```{r load_libraries}
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
library(p8105.datasets)
library(hexbin)
library(ggridges)
```

# Problem 1

__Load dataset__

Firstly, we load the packages and the dataset for setup. 

```{r}
# load NY NOAA dataset
data("ny_noaa")

# In order to assess which data might be an issue, we need to calculate the proportion of missing data for each variable. 
ny_noaa |> 
  summarize(
    across(everything(), ~mean(is.na(.x))) * 100
  )
```

__Dataset description__

The `ny_noaa` dataset contains `r nrow(ny_noaa)` observations and `r ncol(ny_noaa)` variables. The observations were collected from `r n_distinct(ny_noaa$id)` weather stations between date of `r min(ny_noaa$date)` and date of `r max(ny_noaa$date)`. Each observation represents measurements of weather condition from one weather station on a specific date. The variables included in the dataset are station id, date, precipitation, snowfall, snow depth, and daily maximum and minimum temperatures. The proportion of missing data for variables station id, precipitation, snowfall, snow depth, daily maximum temperatures and daily minimum temperatures is 0%, 0%, 5.62%, 14.69%, 22.80%, 43.71% and 43.71%, respectively. Based on this, missing data is a large issue in this dataset, especially for daily maximum and minimum temperatures. There is also moderate missingness for snowfall (14.69% missing) and snow depth (22.80% missing), whereas missing data issue is mild for precipitation. 

__Data cleaning and answer questions__

For data cleaning, I first standardized the variable names. Then, I separated the `date` variable into 3 different variables `year`, `month` and `day`. In the original dataset, the units of temperatures and precipitation are in tenths of degrees Celsius (C) and tenths of millimeters (mm), respectively. I converted the unit of precipitation to mm and the unit of temperatures to degrees C. 

```{r}
# Clean the dataset
library(lubridate) # I found this packages and functions for separating year, month and day on the Internet. 
noaa_cleaned_df = 
  ny_noaa |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  mutate(
    year = year(date), 
    month = month(date), 
    day = day(date), 
    prcp = prcp / 10, 
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10, 
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10
  )

# For snowfall, what are the most commonly observed values? 
noaa_cleaned_df |> 
  filter(!is.na(snow)) |> 
  count(snow, sort = TRUE)
```

0 mm is the most commonly observed value. This is because most days are not in winter and don’t have snowfall. Other common values are 13 mm, 25 mm, 51 mm, and 76 mm. These values are likely the result of converting from inches to millimeters. If converting these values to inches, we can get approximately 0.5 inches, 1 inch, 2 inches, and 3 inches, respectively.

```{r}
# Get the average max temperature in January and in July in each station across years
noaa_cleaned_df |>
  filter(
    month == 1 | month == 7, 
    !is.na(tmax)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    month = case_match(
      month, 
      1 ~ "January", 
      7 ~ "July"
    )
  ) |> 
  group_by(id, year, month) |> 
  summarize(
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax), 
  ) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id)) + 
  geom_line(alpha = 0.4) + 
  facet_grid(. ~ month) + 
  labs(
    title = "Average maximum temperature in January and July by stations, 1981-2010", 
    x = "Year", 
    y = "Average maximum temperature (degrees C)", 
    caption = "Data from the ny_noaa dataset"
  )
```

Observable / interpretable structure: 

Based on the plots, there is a seasonal difference in average maximum temperatures, which is that temperatures in July are much higher than in January. Temperatures in January ranging from -10 to 10 degrees C also have greater fluctuation of average maximum temperatures than temperatures in July ranging from 20-35 degrees C. Most weather stations capture similar annual patterns, but there are a few outliers. For example, the lowest average maximum temperature in July was around 14 degrees C in the late 1980s; the lowest average maximum temperature in January was around -13 degrees C in the early 1980s.

```{r, fig.width=12, fig.height=8}
# Create temperature plot for tmax vs tmin
temperature_plot = 
  noaa_cleaned_df |>
  filter(
    !is.na(tmax), 
    !is.na(tmin)
  ) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) + 
  geom_hex() + 
  labs(
    title = "Temperature plot",
    x = "Minimum daily temperature (degrees C)", 
    y = "Maximum daily temperature (degrees C)"
  )

# Create snowfall distribution plot by year
snowfall_plot = 
  noaa_cleaned_df |> 
  filter(
    snow > 0, 
    snow < 100
  ) |> 
  mutate(year = factor(year)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = snow, y = year)) + 
  geom_density_ridges(
    scale = 1, 
    alpha = 0.7, 
    fill = "skyblue", 
    color = "white"
  ) + 
  labs(
    title = "Snowfall distribution by year",
    x = "Snowfall (mm)",
    y = "Year",
    caption = "Data from the ny_noaa dataset"
  )

# Combine the two plots into a two-panel plot
temperature_plot + snowfall_plot
```

Comments on plots: 

(i) Temperature plot: There is an obvious positive relationship between daily minimum and maximum temperatures. Days with higher minimum daily temperatures also tend to have higher maximum temperatures. Some observations fall outside the main patterns. Some combinations even show a minimum temperature higher than the maximum, which may indicate errors in the records. 

(ii) Distribution of snowfall by year plot: The distributions of snowfall are quite similar across years and do not show major changes in the long term. Most snowfall values are concentrated below 40 mm, and peaks occur repeatedly around approximately 13, 25, 51, and 76 mm across many years. This is consistent with the observation of common values in the previous question, which indicates that the snowfall values may be converted from inches to millimeters. 


# Problem 2

__Load, clean and merge the datasets__

```{r}
# Load and clean demographic data
nhanes_covar_df = 
  read_csv("data/nhanes_covar.csv", skip = 4) |>
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  filter(age >= 21) |> 
  drop_na() |> 
  mutate(
    sex = factor(
      case_match(
        sex, 
        1 ~ "Male", 
        2 ~ "Female"
      ), 
      levels = c("Male", "Female")
    ), 
    education = factor(
      case_match(
        education, 
        1 ~ "Less than high school", 
        2 ~ "High school equivalent", 
        3 ~ "More than high school"
      ), 
      levels = c(
        "Less than high school",
        "High school equivalent",
        "More than high school"
      )
    )
  )

# Load accelerometer data
nhanes_accel_df = 
  read_csv("data/nhanes_accel.csv") |> 
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  pivot_longer(
    min1:min1440, 
    names_to = "minute", 
    names_prefix = "min", 
    values_to = "mims"
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    minute = as.numeric(minute)
  )

# Merge two datasets
nhanes_merged_df = 
  inner_join(
    nhanes_covar_df, 
    nhanes_accel_df, 
    by = "seqn"
  )
```
The demographic data requires more data cleaning steps. After loading the demographic data, I firstly cleaned it by standardizing variable names followed by filtering and retaining participants aged 21 or above. Then, observations with missing data were dropped. The numeric codes for sex and education were then converted to categorical factors and ordered as `Male` / `Female` for sex and `Less than high school` / `High school equivalent` / `More than high school` for education. I then loaded the accelerometer data and cleaned the variable names. The accelerometer data were then tidied by reshaping the `min1`-`min1440` variables into long format, creating separate `minute`and `mims` variables, and converting `minute` to numeric. Finally, I merged the two datasets by participant ID, `seqn`, using the `inner_join()` function. 

__Table and visualization__

```{r}
# Produce a reader-friendly table for the number of men and women in each education category
nhanes_merged_df |> 
  distinct(seqn, education, sex) |> 
  group_by(education, sex) |>
  summarize(count = n()) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sex,
    values_from = count
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()
```
Comment: The more than high school group had the largest number of participants, while the less than high school group had the fewest participants. The numbers of men and women were similar in these two education categories, but the high school equivalent group included more men than women. 

```{r}
# Create a visualization of the age distributions for men and women in each education category
nhanes_merged_df |> 
  distinct(seqn, sex, age, education) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = sex, y = age)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill = sex)) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  labs(
    title = "Age Distribution by Sex and Education Level",
    x = "Sex",
    y = "Age (years)",
    fill = "Sex"
  )
```

Comment: Age distribution is different across education levels. Among participants with less than a high school education, the median ages of men and women are similar, both around 60 years old. In the high school equivalent group, women generally have higher age than men, and their median age is also higher than men. Participants with more than a high school education are relatively younger, with median ages in the early 40s for both men and women. There are no obvious outliers. 

__Plot total activities vs. age__

```{r}
nhanes_merged_df |>
  group_by(seqn, sex, age, education) |>
  summarize(
    total_activity = sum(mims, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = age,
      y = total_activity,
      color = sex
    )
  ) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  labs(
    title = "Total daily activity by age, sex, and education Level",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Total daily activity",
    color = "Sex"
  )
```

Comment: Across all three education levels, total daily activity generally decreased with age, although the trend was not completely linear. Among participants with less than a high school education, men and women showed similar patterns. Compared with other education groups, they had the highest activity levels at younger ages and a steeper overall decline. Among those with a high school equivalent education, women tend to have higher total daily activity than men, with the largest sex difference around age 40, but this gap narrowed at older ages. Among participants with more than a high school education, total daily activity levels were relatively similar between men and women, but women's activity levels seem to be higher than men's.
